analysis.one_liner: Requires the loser of a negligence lawsuit to pay the winner's attorneys' fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced the losing side in any lawsuit over injuries or property damage caused by negligence to pay the winning side's legal bills, in both state and federal courts, unless a judge found special circumstances making that unjust. It was introduced on January 4, 1995, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never moved again. No committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would have been defendants in injury lawsuits — typically businesses, insurers, doctors, manufacturers, and property owners — who could have shifted their legal bills onto people who sued them and lost. Prevailing plaintiffs could also recover fees, but the practical effect of a loser-pays rule falls hardest on people deciding whether to sue: someone hurt by a negligent company would have had to weigh not just losing the case but owing a corporation's legal fees. That risk tends to deter lawsuits, including ones with merit, which is exactly what deep-pocketed defendants and their insurers want.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses and insurers defending injury lawsuits

how_it_helps.text: Any prevailing party in a civil suit for money damages for personal injury, death, or property loss from negligence — plaintiff or defendant — would have been entitled to a court-awarded reasonable attorney's fee from the losing side, in state and federal courts alike.

A judge could refuse to award fees only by finding special circumstances that would make the award unjust, leaving little room to screen out cases where the fee risk would be crushing for an individual.

The design is the classic 'loser pays' (English rule) model: by attaching a large financial penalty to losing, it discourages filing suits the filer might lose. That benefits insured and corporate defendants, who face many more injury claims than they file, more than it benefits individual plaintiffs.

analysis.who_pays: People who file negligence lawsuits and lose would owe the other side's legal fees. Because individuals suing over injuries usually have far less money than the companies and insurers they sue, the threat of a fee award would fall on them and would deter many people — including those with legitimate but hard-to-prove claims — from going to court at all. The bill would also have overridden the traditional American practice, in which each side pays its own legal fees, in state courts across the country.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured people who sue and lose

drawbacks.text: A person with a real but uncertain injury claim could face paying a corporation's or insurer's entire legal bill if they lost, a risk far larger for an individual of modest means than for an insured business. Legal scholars across the spectrum recognize that loser-pays rules deter not just frivolous suits but meritorious ones, and the bill's only escape valve — 'special circumstances' — was left undefined.

The bill was a one-size-fits-all mandate: it applied to every negligence damages suit in every state court, overriding whatever fee rules states had chosen for themselves, with no exception for small claims where the fee exposure would dwarf the amount in dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Discouraging truly meritless lawsuits is a genuine goal, and letting a winning plaintiff recover fees could help some injured people afford counsel. But the structure is lopsided: the parties most exposed to being sued over negligence are businesses and insurers, and the people deciding whether to sue are usually individuals betting limited savings on an uncertain outcome. The bill offered no income-based protection, no small-claim exception, and no definition of when 'special circumstances' would excuse an award, so its most predictable effect was fewer injury cases — including valid ones — ever reaching a courtroom.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a vote, or any other action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative F. James Sensenbrenner Jr. introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress, with one Republican cosponsor.

The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; that referral is the last action in the bill's entire history, meaning the committee never marked it up, reported it, or sent it to the floor.
The bill died quietly when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the existing rule — each side in a lawsuit pays its own attorneys' fees — remained in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who might sue over an injury kept the current system, in which losing a lawsuit does not automatically mean owing the other side's legal fees. Businesses and insurers gained nothing, but lost nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who might sue over injuries

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the loser-pays fee-shifting bill on the first day of the 104th Congress.

for.name: One House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor; no Democrat did.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Henry Hyde (R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no split can be measured; the only support on record was Republican (the sponsor plus one cosponsor), and no one on record opposed it.

industries.note: A loser-pays rule would have let them shift legal costs onto people who sued them and lost, and the fee risk would deter many injury claims before they were filed. Their gain comes directly from fewer injured people recovering in court.

Clients would have faced paying the defendant's fees if they lost, making people far more reluctant to hire a lawyer over a negligence claim, and contingency practice would have carried new risk. Their interest in the bill's failure ran alongside injured people's access to the courts.
